title: Merton's mountain
hookLine: a young writer becomes a Trappist monk and writes about contemplation and peace

cards: A young man in New York has tried what a clever young writer can try: parties, politics, poetry, ambition. He becomes a Catholic, and then he goes further.
He travels to a monastery in the Kentucky hills called Gethsemani and asks to join the Trappists, monks who live by prayer, work and long stretches of silence. His name is Thomas Merton.
Later he tells the story of that road in a memoir called The Seven Storey Mountain. Today closes a week of voices with the monk who climbed into silence, and what he found waiting there.

teach.b: You might expect a monk's message to be: leave the world behind. Merton wrote about contemplation, which he describes as a kind of waking up: becoming aware of God's life, the reality underneath all the noise.
And he kept insisting it isn't a prize reserved for monks.
Years into monastic life, he's sent into the city of Louisville on an errand.

Standing on a busy corner in the shopping district, surrounded by strangers, he writes that he was suddenly overwhelmed with the realization that he loved all these people, that they were his and he theirs, that they could not be alien to one another even though they were total strangers.
He compares it to waking from a dream of separateness. The monk who left the world found it again on a shopping street. Silence wasn't a wall against people.
It was where he learned to see them.
A psalm puts the invitation in a handful of words: "Be still, and know that I am God." Merton's life reads like a long commentary on its first two words.
He went on to write about peace, war and racial justice, the same stillness turned outward.
Look back over this week of voices: MacDonald's love that won't let go, Barth's song, Bonhoeffer's question, Tillich's concern, the serenity prayer, Weil's attention.
And Merton, finding the crowd at the end of the silence.

how: Some Christians set aside time for silent contemplative prayer, alone or in groups, and some go on retreat at monasteries such as Gethsemani; Merton's books are read by Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox Christians alike.

games.q: you've given up the city for a monastery's silence. years later you're sent back into town on an errand, and you're standing on a busy corner. what happens?
o: you feel above the shoppers rushing past.
you're overwhelmed with love for the strangers around you.
you hurry back to the monastery as fast as you can.
games.why: Merton wrote that he suddenly loved all these people, as if waking from a dream of separateness. the silence had taught him to see them.

practice: No words for this one, no list to work through: let the sounds of the room come and go, and when a thought arrives, let it pass like a car on the street outside, heard and then gone.
If you pray, you can rest in the line be still, and know that I am God, then let even that go quiet; if you don't, simply be still.

wordCard.voice: Merton's mountain. Thomas Merton's climb into a monastery's silence, where he found contemplation, and found the world waiting there too.

orig.note: Latin: contemplation, the word Merton's Catholic tradition uses for prayer that rests in God.

carryVoice: Your line: contemplation is for all. Not a prize kept for monks. Same time tomorrow.
